headings.title: Introduction to Intravenous Therapy
headings.content: Intravenous therapy is a core nursing competency that involves the direct administration of fluids, medications, electrolytes, and blood products into a patient's venous system. In the context of nursing practice in Nigeria and globally, mastering IV therapy ensures rapid therapeutic onset, making it vital in emergency situations, surgical interventions, and critical care management. Unlike oral or intramuscular routes, IV administration bypasses the digestive system and first-pass metabolism, delivering 100% bioavailability of the prescribed substance directly into the systemic circulation. As nursing students, understanding the pharmacological and physiological rationale behind IV therapy is fundamental. You must appreciate that while this route offers immediate action, it also carries higher risks of adverse reactions, such as rapid toxicity or systemic infection, due to the direct access to the bloodstream. Strict adherence to aseptic technique, precise mathematical calculations for infusion rates, and continuous patient monitoring are non-negotiable standards of safe nursing care. Throughout your clinical placements in Nigerian healthcare facilities, you will routinely initiate, monitor, and discontinue intravenous lines. Therefore, developing both theoretical mastery and practical dexterity early in your training will build your clinical confidence and protect your patients from preventable harm. Remember that every IV procedure requires informed consent, patient education, and constant evaluation of the fluid balance status to prevent complications like fluid overload.

headings.title: Indications and Contraindications for IV Injections
headings.content: Before initiating intravenous therapy, nurses must thoroughly evaluate the patient to establish clear clinical indications and rule out any contraindications. Indications for IV injections include rapid drug action in emergencies, correction of severe electrolyte and fluid imbalances, administration of blood or blood products, delivery of total parenteral nutrition (TPN), and situations where the patient cannot tolerate oral intake due to persistent vomiting or unconsciousness. In Nigerian clinical settings, patients presenting with severe dehydration from malaria, gastroenteritis, or cholera frequently require immediate IV fluid resuscitation. Conversely, contraindications must be meticulously assessed to prevent patient harm. Absolute contraindications include severe localized trauma, burns, or infection directly over the intended puncture site, as inserting a cannula through compromised skin introduces bacteria into deep tissues and the bloodstream. Relative contraindications involve choosing an extremity with compromised circulation, such as an arm affected by lymphedema following a radical mastectomy, an arteriovenous fistula used for hemodialysis, or an extremity with chronic venous stasis. Nurses must also check for known patient allergies to components of the infusion, such as latex in gloves or specific additives in medications. Clinical judgment dictates selecting alternative sites or routes, such as the unaffected contralateral limb, when contraindications are present in a primary site.

headings.title: Equipment and Supplies Preparation
headings.content: Proper preparation of equipment and supplies before initiating an intravenous cannulation procedure promotes efficiency, minimizes patient discomfort, and maintains a sterile field. As a nursing student, you should gather all required items before approaching the patient's bedside to avoid leaving the patient unattended once the procedure has begun. Essential supplies include an appropriately sized IV cannula (typically gauge 18G to 24G depending on patient age and vein caliber), a tourniquet, an alcohol swab or chlorhexidine antiseptic solution, sterile gauze, transparent semi-permeable dressings or adhesive tape, non-sterile gloves, an extension set or primed IV infusion tubing, and the prescribed IV fluid bag. Additionally, a sharps container must be readily accessible at the bedside to ensure safe disposal of needles immediately after use. Before opening any sterile package, inspect the items for integrity, ensuring packaging is intact, unexpired, and uncontaminated. Prime your IV infusion tubing by filling the drip chamber halfway and flushing all air bubbles out of the tubing to prevent air embolism. Organize your workspace logically so that every item is within arm's reach. Preparing your equipment methodically reflects professional competence and significantly reduces procedural anxiety for both you and the patient.

headings.title: Anatomy and Selection of Peripheral Veins
headings.content: Selecting an appropriate peripheral vein is critical for successful IV cannulation and the prevention of mechanical phlebitis or infiltration. As a nurse, you should begin your assessment distal on the upper extremities and move proximally for subsequent insertions, preserving upper sites for future use. Common sites include the metacarpal veins on the dorsal surface of the hand, the cephalic and basilic veins in the forearm, and the median cubital vein in the antecubital fossa. However, the antecubital fossa should be avoided for long-term infusions because flexion of the elbow can kink the cannula and dislodge it. Ideal veins feel bouncy, resilient, and refill when gently palpated; they should be straight and visible rather than sclerosed, tortuous, or hard. In pediatric and neonatal nursing, scalp veins or foot veins may occasionally be utilized, though lower extremity veins are generally avoided in adults due to the heightened risk of thrombophlebitis and sluggish circulation. Factors influencing vein selection include the patient's age, clinical status, prescribed therapy type, and vein condition. For example, viscous solutions like blood products require larger gauge cannulas (e.g., 18G or 20G) placed in larger forearm veins, whereas fragile veins in elderly patients necessitate smaller gauges (e.g., 22G or 24G) combined with gentle handling to prevent vessel rupture.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for IV Cannulation
headings.content: Executing a step-by-step procedure for IV cannulation requires precision, patience, and strict adherence to infection control protocols. Begin by verifying the doctor's prescription, explaining the procedure to the patient, and performing hand hygiene before donning non-invasive gloves. Apply the tourniquet approximately 10 to 15 centimeters above the selected site to engorge the vein, and palpate to confirm your target. Cleanse the skin using an approved antiseptic swab (such as 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol) using a friction scrub for at least 30 seconds, and allow it to dry completely to maximize antimicrobial effectiveness. Anchor the vein by pulling the skin taut distally with your non-dominant hand. Hold the IV catheter with the bevel facing upward at a 15 to 30-degree angle, depending on the vein's depth, and pierce the skin smoothly. Watch for a 'flashback' of dark red blood in the flashback chamber, which confirms needle entry into the lumen. Once flashback appears, lower the catheter almost parallel to the skin and advance the entire unit slightly further to ensure the catheter itself is inside the vessel. Advance the plastic catheter off the needle while withdrawing the stylet simultaneously, never re-sheathing the needle to avoid needle-stick injuries. Release the tourniquet, connect your primed extension set or infusion tubing, secure the hub with a transparent sterile dressing, and flush gently to confirm patency.

headings.title: Administration of IV Medications and Fluids
headings.content: The safe administration of intravenous medications and fluids is a critical daily responsibility for nurses. Once IV access is established and confirmed patent, you must calculate and regulate infusion rates with utmost mathematical precision. Formulas using drops per minute (gtt/min) based on the administration set's drop factor (e.g., 15 gtt/mL for standard sets or 60 gtt/mL for microdrip sets) or milliters per hour (mL/hr) for electronic infusion pumps must be applied accurately. Rapid infusion of certain medications, such as potassium chloride or high-dose intravenous push opioids, can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias or severe respiratory depression, making rate verification mandatory. Always perform the 'five rights' of medication administration (right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time) combined with compatibility checks. Many IV medications are chemically incompatible and will precipitate if mixed in the same line, causing vascular occlusion or adverse drug reactions; therefore, flush lines with normal saline between incompatible medications or use secondary intermittent infusion sets (piggybacks). Continuously monitor the infusion site for signs of infiltration, such as swelling, coolness, or pain, which indicate that fluid is leaking into surrounding subcutaneous tissue rather than entering the vein. Patient education regarding reporting burning sensations or discomfort at the site enhances safety and early complication detection.

headings.title: Monitoring and Maintenance of IV Sites
headings.content: Continuous monitoring and routine maintenance of peripheral intravenous sites are essential nursing duties to ensure therapy continuity and prevent nosocomial complications. Nurses must inspect the IV site every shift, or more frequently for high-risk patients or vesicant infusions. Assessment parameters include checking for redness, swelling, local warmth, tenderness, leakage around the insertion site, and patency of the infusion. Dressings must be clean, dry, and securely intact; if a dressing becomes lifted, soiled, or damp, it must be changed immediately using strict aseptic technique. According to international and national infection control guidelines, peripheral IV cannula sites should be routinely rotated every 72 to 96 hours, or sooner if clinical indications of complications arise. However, site rotation should be guided by clinical assessment and facility policy rather than blind adherence, particularly in patients with difficult venous access. Extension sets, intermittent injection caps, and continuous infusion tubing must also be changed according to institutional infection prevention protocols (typically every 96 hours for continuous lines). Documenting the condition of the IV site, the infusion rate, and any fluid volume infused forms an integral part of maintaining accurate patient records and ensures multidisciplinary team awareness.

headings.title: Complications of Intravenous Therapy and Management
headings.content: Intravenous therapy carries inherent risks of local and systemic complications that require prompt recognition and expert nursing management. Local complications include infiltration (fluid leaking into surrounding tissue), extravasation (vesicant medication leaking into tissue causing necrosis), phlebitis (inflammation of the vein wall characterized by pain, erythema, and a palpable cord), thrombophlebitis (blood clot combined with inflammation), and local hematoma formation. If infiltration or extravasation occurs, the nurse must immediately stop the infusion, disconnect the tubing, remove the cannula, elevate the affected limb, and apply warm or cold compresses as dictated by the specific medication protocol. Systemic complications are more dangerous and include circulatory overload (manifested by dyspnea, hypertension, crackles in lungs, and jugular venous distention), air embolism (caused by air entering the vascular system, presenting with sudden chest pain, cyanosis, and hypotension), and catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI) characterized by fever, chills, and purulent drainage. Managing systemic emergencies requires immediate cessation of the infusion, notifying the physician, administering emergency oxygen or medications, and placing the patient in an appropriate posture, such as the Trendelenburg position on the left side for suspected air embolism to trap air in the right ventricle.

headings.title: Discontinuation of Intravenous Access
headings.content: Discontinuation of intravenous access is a routine nursing procedure performed when therapy is completed, the site develops complications, or the patient is transitioned to oral medications. To discontinue an IV line safely, explain the procedure to the patient, perform hand hygiene, and put on gloves. Clamp the infusion tubing and gently peel away the transparent dressing and adhesive tape toward the insertion site to avoid pulling the catheter out prematurely. Place a piece of sterile gauze or cotton ball lightly over the insertion site without applying pressure yet. Withdraw the cannula smoothly and steadily along the exact angle of insertion to prevent trauma to the vein wall and surrounding tissues. Immediately inspect the removed catheter to ensure the tip is intact; a sheared catheter tip is a medical emergency that can lead to a pulmonary embolism. Apply firm, direct pressure to the puncture site using sterile gauze for at least two to three minutes (or longer if the patient has a bleeding disorder or is on anticoagulant therapy) to achieve hemostasis. Secure a clean adhesive bandage over the site once bleeding has stopped. Finally, document the reason for discontinuation, the condition of the removed cannula tip, the patient's tolerance, and the integrity of the site in the nursing notes.

headings.title: Documentation and Legal Responsibilities in Nursing
headings.content: Documentation and legal responsibilities are foundational aspects of safe, professional nursing practice in intravenous therapy. Every action related to IV cannulation, medication administration, site maintenance, and discontinuation must be accurately and promptly recorded in the patient's official medical record. Documentation must include the date and time of insertion, the brand and gauge of the catheter used, the exact anatomical site selected, the number of insertion attempts, the type of fluids or medications infused, and the patient's tolerance to the procedure. Legally, nurses are held accountable for their clinical actions under both professional nursing codes and civil law; performing IV therapy without adequate training or failing to monitor a patient receiving vesicant medications constitutes negligence and malpractice. In Nigerian healthcare practice, keeping contemporaneous, clear, and objective notes protects both the patient and the nurse in legal inquiries. If an adverse event occurs, such as infiltration or medication extravasation, an incident report must be completed in accordance with hospital policy, distinct from the clinical chart. Always remember the golden nursing rule: if it was not documented, legally, it was not done.
